summaries.example: Imagine two students trying to guess the next 10 cards in a shuffled deck. Maya writes her guesses before seeing any cards and gets all 10 right. Leo sees the first 9 cards, then writes those 9 down and guesses the tenth. Maya's success seems more surprising. But philosophers ask whether it is really better evidence, or whether it only tells us that Maya may have used a more reliable way of guessing.
summaries.summary: This entry examines whether a scientific theory deserves more support when it predicts evidence than when it is adjusted to fit evidence already known. A theory that predicts a new result may seem impressive because it risked being wrong. This idea is called predictivism. Some versions say predictions are always better; others say they are better only in certain situations. Philosophers disagree about what makes a result “new.” It might be unknown when the theory was created, not used in building it, or not explained by rival theories. The entry discusses several explanations for the apparent advantage of prediction. Prediction may show that a method is reliable, avoid a poorly fitted or “fudged” theory, reduce the risk of overfitting, or pass a difficult test. Critics argue that the advantage may come from other facts, such as a theory having independent support before the evidence appeared. The entry also considers how this debate connects with the question of whether successful scientific theories are approximately true.
key_ideas: Scientists often value theories that correctly predict surprising results.
Some philosophers think prediction is better evidence because it may show a reliable way of discovering things.
Other philosophers think the important issue is not the timing, but whether the theory is simple, connected, testable, and well supported.
There are different kinds of novelty, so there is no single easy rule about all predictions and accommodations.
The debate also affects scientific realism, the view that successful scientific theories may describe the world approximately truthfully.
summaries.why_it_matters: Scientists use evidence to decide which explanations deserve trust. Learning about prediction and accommodation helps us notice that a good-looking match is not always enough. We should ask how a theory was made, what else supports it, whether it could have failed, and whether its success might be luck. These questions help us think carefully about scientific reasoning without assuming that one simple rule settles every case.

important_terms.definition: A prediction is a claim about what will happen or be found before the evidence is known or used.
An accommodation is a theory or claim changed or made to fit evidence that is already known.
Predictivism is the view that evidence can support a theory more when the theory predicted it than when it was made to fit it.
A hypothesis is a proposed explanation that can be tested against evidence.
Ad hoc means made for one special problem, sometimes in a way that does not connect well with the rest of a theory.
Novel evidence is evidence that is new in some relevant way, such as not being used to build the theory.

questions_to_think_about: If someone changes a guess after seeing the answer, should that count as evidence that the guess was good?
Could a prediction be lucky rather than produced by a reliable method?
What makes a scientific test genuinely difficult for a theory to pass?
Is a theory better because it predicted a result, or because the theory explains the result well?

summaries.example: Suppose two researchers propose models of a disease. Researcher A develops a model using an initial set of patient data, then correctly forecasts results in a later, untouched set. Researcher B sees the entire data set first and adjusts a flexible model until it fits every case. A's success seems more impressive, but the comparison is not automatic. A may have used a reliable method, while B may have overfit noise. Yet a fit made from existing data can still provide evidence if the hypothesis was constrained in ways that would have failed if it were false. The philosophical question is which features of the case explain the difference in support.
summaries.summary: The entry analyzes the philosophical dispute over whether prediction has greater evidential value than accommodation. In the original historical contrast, a prediction is an empirical consequence not yet verified when a theory is formed, whereas an accommodation is a consequence already known or used in constructing the theory. Predictivism can be global or local, and strong or weak. Strong predictivism says prediction is inherently superior; weak versions say predictive success indicates another valuable feature, such as reliability, coherence, or resistance to overfitting. The entry surveys competing accounts. Maher's reliable-method approach treats a long series of successful predictions as evidence that the method was not merely guessing. The fudging approach emphasizes that accommodations may be forced into conflict with background beliefs. Lange focuses on arbitrary conjunctions, in which support for one part does not spread to another. Mayo argues that the central issue is severity: a hypothesis can sometimes be use-constructed and still be very unlikely to fit if false. Worrall distinguishes unconditional confirmation of a theory's core from conditional support for a version whose parameters were fixed by the data. Hitchcock and Sober use model complexity and the Akaike approach to explain why prediction can sometimes indicate less overfitting, but not always. Barnes shifts attention from how a theory was discovered to what grounds a scientist's endorsement and how predictive success may confirm background beliefs. The entry also presents anti-predictivist arguments and explains why novel success has been important in debates about scientific realism, including the no-miracles argument and responses to pessimistic induction.
key_ideas: Historical defenders of prediction argued that successful novel results are unlikely to be accidental, while critics argued that prior reasons for proposing a theory may be doing the real evidential work.
Novelty has several meanings: temporal novelty, problem-novelty, use-novelty, knowledge-based novelty, and novelty relative to competing theories.
The null support thesis says that evidence used to build a theory gives it no support. Critics challenge this with statistical examples and argue that a theory can still face a demanding test.
Several weak predictivist accounts explain predictive advantage through reliable discovery methods, coherence, avoidance of arbitrary conjunctions, severe testing, or protection against overfitting.

Some theories distinguish a theory's broad core from auxiliary assumptions and parameters. Evidence used to set a parameter may support the resulting version only conditionally, not the core by itself.

Anti-predictivists argue that apparent predictive superiority may result from unequal prior support, background beliefs, or other features rather than prediction itself. The debate matters to arguments for scientific realism.
summaries.why_it_matters: The issue concerns how evidence should change rational confidence in scientific theories. A theory that fits known data may be impressive, misleading, or both, depending on how constrained it was and what independent reasons support it. A successful prediction may indicate truth, a reliable method, a non-arbitrary structure, or simply a favorable circumstance. Separating these possibilities prevents the slogan “prediction is always better” from replacing careful analysis. The debate also shows why judgments about scientific realism depend not only on success, but on what kind of success a theory has and what alternatives are available.

important_terms.definition: Predictivism is the view that evidence confirms a theory more strongly when the theory predicted that evidence than when the theory was constructed to accommodate it.
Global predictivism says prediction is always superior to accommodation; local predictivism says the advantage occurs only in some cases.
Strong predictivism treats prediction as intrinsically better, while weak predictivism treats it as a sign of another epistemically valuable feature.
Use-novelty concerns whether evidence was used to construct a theory, regardless of when the evidence became known.
A severe test is one that a hypothesis would be unlikely to pass if it were false.
Overfitting occurs when a model is made to match noisy data too closely and therefore performs poorly on new data.
Conditional confirmation supports a specific version of a theory only if there is independent support for the broader core theory.
Scientific realism is the position that successful mature scientific theories are at least approximately true.

questions_to_think_about: Does the time at which evidence became known have epistemic importance, or is the theory-evidence relationship what matters?
Can a theory constructed from data nevertheless pass a severe test?
When does adding an auxiliary hypothesis count as a legitimate refinement rather than an ad hoc rescue?
Should predictive success support a theory's truth, the reliability of its method, or only some part of its structure?
How might overfitting explain some—but not all—cases in which prediction seems superior?

summaries.example: A weather team creates a storm model. Team A makes its forecast before the storm arrives and correctly predicts several unusual changes in wind direction. Team B waits until much of the storm has happened, then adjusts its model so that it matches the recorded path. Team A's success seems stronger because the model could have failed. Still, Team B's model might be useful if its rules were fixed by a good theory and the match would have been unlikely if the model were wrong. Philosophers ask what exactly makes A's evidence stronger, and whether that reason applies in every case.
summaries.summary: This entry asks whether scientists should give extra credit to theories that predict evidence rather than merely accommodate it. A prediction is normally understood as a consequence not yet verified when the theory is formed; an accommodation fits evidence already known. The view that predictions are superior is called predictivism, but it has several forms. Global predictivism says the advantage is general, whereas local predictivism limits it to particular cases. Strong predictivism says prediction is valuable in itself. Weak predictivism says it is valuable because it often signals something else, such as a dependable discovery method or a theory that was not patched together after seeing the data. The entry traces the debate through ideas about ad hoc hypotheses and different kinds of novelty. It also examines the null support thesis, the claim that evidence used to construct a theory supports it not at all. Critics argue that this conclusion is too strong: a use-constructed hypothesis can still be tested in a way it would probably fail if false. Other accounts focus on severe tests, arbitrary combinations of claims, background beliefs, and the danger of overfitting noisy observations. Anti-predictivists, drawing on arguments associated with Keynes and Howson, suggest that prior reasons for favoring a theory may explain why predictive success appears more impressive. Finally, the entry connects novel success with scientific realism. Realists use successful novel predictions in arguing that theories are approximately true; critics point to historically successful theories that were later rejected or to the possibility that only some parts of a theory are supported.
key_ideas: Prediction seems valuable because a theory that takes a risk and succeeds may reveal more than a theory adjusted after the fact.
Philosophers disagree about novelty. A result can be new because it was unknown, not used, not part of the original problem, or not explained by rival theories.
Some predictivists defend a limited claim: predictive success matters because it suggests reliable methods, coherent theories, difficult tests, or less overfitting.
The idea that accommodated evidence gives zero support is controversial. Statistical reasoning shows that a hypothesis built from data can sometimes still be strongly supported.
Critics argue that prediction may look better because the predicting theory had stronger independent reasons or because the accommodating theory had extra adjustable assumptions.
Novel predictions are used in arguments about whether science succeeds because its theories are approximately true, but historical examples and rival explanations make that conclusion debated.
summaries.why_it_matters: The debate teaches an important lesson about evidence: the same match between a theory and data can have different meanings depending on how the theory was formed and tested. It also shows that philosophers do not simply divide into people who like predictions and people who dislike them. Many accept that predictive success can matter while disagreeing about why it matters, how much it matters, and whether the reason applies broadly. This careful approach is useful whenever we judge forecasts, models, or explanations.

important_terms.definition: A prediction is a testable claim made before the relevant evidence is known or used in forming the theory.
An accommodation is a theory or modification designed to fit evidence that is already known.
Predictivism is the position that predicted evidence gives stronger support than accommodated evidence, at least in some cases.
A novel result is new relative to some standard, such as the time of construction, the problem the theory addressed, or the evidence used to build it.
An ad hoc hypothesis is an added claim introduced to solve a particular difficulty; it may be criticized when it lacks independent tests or fits poorly with the wider theory.
A research programme is a developing series of theories with central commitments and supporting assumptions that may be revised as evidence changes.
A severe test is a test that a false hypothesis would be unlikely to pass.
Scientific realism is the view that successful scientific theories are at least approximately true, including claims about things we cannot directly observe.

questions_to_think_about: Why might a theory that fits old evidence be less impressive than one that forecasts new evidence?
Can a result be novel even if the scientist knew it before writing the theory?
How can we tell the difference between a useful adjustment and an ad hoc rescue?
Would a prediction made by a random guess deserve much support if it happened to be correct?
What does predictive success show: truth, reliability, or only that a theory survived a test?
